item.title: Woman who rescued injured crow keeps getting 'thank-you gifts' from birds [video]
item.description:
Source: www.youtube.com

Top Comment:

My late father developed a feeding ritual for a crow that lasted for over a decade and was prompted entirely by the crow’s decision to stand in a particular position, which he would only do if he observed my father in the kitchen. It happened a few times a week on the crow’s own schedule, the same way every time.

There were no gifts but over the years we did witness this crow clearly trying to teach its very dependent growing child how to work the human. Ultimately it never succeeded, and we presume this crow eventually either passed on or moved on. But one of the gaggle of jealous magpies who observed the process did take up the role. Being more timid it didn’t simply stand and wait, but would appear, circle the feeding spot until it got my father’s attention, fly up to one specific branch and wait, but otherwise repeat the process it observed. That went on for a couple of years.

The process itself varied according to what food was thrown out, but the crow slowly developed a particularly clever strategy for carrying off whole stale bread crusts by dragging it to a water bowl, moistening then trimming and diagonally cutting a slot into the bread from one corner almost all the way to the other, such that it could hang either side of the beak in a balanced fashion; the magpie that took over learned this by observation and attempted it from day one.

item.title: I Love Software Rendering
item.description:
Source: www.jamesfmackenzie.com

Top Comment:

This isn't software rendering, it's called turning off spatial anti-aliasing. You can still do that in the modernest of modern games. Software rendering went out of the window because the CPU tends to have other things to do whilst playing the game besides only multiplying 4x4 matrices, which was shifted to the shader cores of GPUs. The look-and-feel that the author is discussing including shadow and texture LUTs can also be done on GPUs by passing the tables in to shaders as constant read-only storage buffers; that is not specific to software rendering. It bears mentioning that many modern software renderers (LLVMpipe/Lavapipe, OpenSWR, WARP) are basically full D3D/OpenGL/Vulkan devices in their own right, including shader compilers.

Also, modern spatial anti-aliasing works by multisampling within a pixel (or even neighbouring pixels) and taking the average, rather than filtering across singly-sampled pixels, which massively reduces the quality. Not to mention temporal and machine learning AA techniques including DLSS, XeSS, FSR, and all the TAA implementations in many games.

item.title: Two-Stack Sliding-Window Aggregation
item.description:
Source: orlp.net

Top Comment:

As you suspected, there's some older literature on this, from the 1990s in image processing. There it's not based on stacks or queues but on splitting the output into blocks with the same size as the (constant-length) window. It's sometimes called the van Herk/Gil-Werman algorithm after two sets of independent discoverers; of the two papers I prefer "Computing 2-D Min, Median, and Max Filters" by Gil and Werman which spends just a paragraph on the 1-D windowed operation in section II.

I don't know who first described this as a streaming version but I like the presentation at https://signalsmith-audio.co.uk/writing/2022/constant-time-p... . It is indeed too obscure considering how useful it is!

item.title: Thank You, Deno
item.description:
Source: www.vlt.io

Top Comment:

> Deno 1.0 shipped in 2020 on the original terms, & then spent the next four years walking them back one piece at a time. First the deps.ts convention, one file that re-exported every URL: a manifest in all but name. Then lock.json, an integrity hash per URL: a lockfile. Then import maps, so you could write bare specifiers again.

I object to two of these categorisations.

deps.ts was a convention, not a built-in runtime feature. If you want to follow the convention, that's fine. It's just a regular old typescript file!

Import maps were not Deno walking back, but implementing a web platform feature. Parity with browser JS was a standout feature of Deno from the beginning. This was walking forwards if anything.

However, broadly, the story is indeed one of Deno moving away from its opinionated roots towards pragmatism (drop-in replacement for Node).

item.description:
Source: github.com

Top Comment:

After the OAI demo, like many others, I tried to use KiCAD through computer-use. This doesn't produce great results.

I have found the best results through a mix of Happy[0], this repo, and computer use to fill in the blanks.

It is _really_ good at the stackup and part config, but creates some absolutely terrible routes. It will snake tiny traces through some SMD pins even though there is plenty of space available outside of the component. When it hits an obstacle, instead of creating 2 45 degree turns, it does 10~30 small ones creating some sort of weird crooked arc.

I have produced a couple of boards for testing this way and they are generally functional.

I have tried KiCadRoutingTools[1] as well which does seem to create routes that make more sense.

Anyone any better experiences with these or similar tools?
